'''Louise Doris Adams''' (2 July 1889&nbsp;– 24 December 1965) was a British [[mathematics education|mathematics educator]] and [[Ofsted#Inspectors|school inspector]] (HMI) who wrote the 1953 book ''A Background to Primary School Mathematics'' ([[Oxford University Press]]){{r|cook|edres}} and became president of the [[Mathematical Association]] for 1959.{{r|pres}}

==Life==
Adams earned a degree from [[Bedford College, London]], with second-class honours in mathematics in 1911.{{r|obit|ulhr}}
Her work as an inspector was centred on the [[West Country]] and particularly [[Bristol]]; she retired from the inspectorate in 1950.{{r|obit}}

She joined the [[Mathematical Association]] in approximately 1915, and was a member for 51 years;{{r|obit}} she became a member of the Teaching Sub-Committee of the Mathematical Association in 1946, of which she became Chairman in 1954 and remained a member until her death.{{r|melrose}} She was also a member of the Applications, Arithmetic and Secondary Modern Sub-Committees.
When she became president of the Mathematical Association in 1959, she became only the second woman to hold that office since the association's founding in 1871, after [[Mary Cartwright]] in 1951,{{r|pres|obit}} and the second HMI, after W. C. Fletcher in 1939.{{r|pres|rollett}}

She died in 1965.{{r|obit}}

==Contributions==
Adams had "considerable experience as a teacher and inspector" and wrote her book, ''A Background to Primary School Mathematics'' (1953), on the basis of that experience.{{r|edres}} It was aimed at teachers of primary-school mathematics, and used case studies from approximately 80 students to advocate linking the teaching of mathematics to the individual experiences of the students.{{r|cook}} Her book "inspired many teachers" and prefigured a greater emphasis on play with mathematical tools over [[rote learning]].{{r|breakell}}

As a member of the Teaching Sub-Committee of the Mathematical Association, Adams helped shift the association's focus "from teaching to learning"{{r|breakell}} and from what should be taught to how it should be taught, and promoted the inclusion of primary as well as secondary education within the project's scope.{{r|obit}} Both her book and her presidential address to the Mathematical Association were a major impetus to the reform of mathematical education in the UK, as was the Teaching Sub-Committee's 1955 report ''The Teaching of Mathematics in Primary Schools'', which she was instrumental in writing.{{r|breakell}}{{r|obit}}
